course.title: Software Design and Architecture
course.description: Learn how to shape software so that it stays easy to change: hide decisions, draw boundaries, choose between architecture styles, and record why.
course.audience: A capable adult who can read short Python and has written or reviewed some code. Assumes CS Basics and Python for Data Analysis. System Design is the companion course: it sizes systems for load and failure, while this one structures the code and the boundaries between services. This course states architecture-style trade-offs and refers to System Design for their mechanics, and System Design does not repeat the style comparison.

paragraphs: A program that works today can still be hard to change tomorrow, and over the life of most software the cost of changing it is the larger cost. Some decisions are cheap to revisit, such as the name of a variable inside one function, while others become expensive the moment other code depends on them, such as the shape of the data a service sends out or the rule about which module may call which. Software architecture is the study of that second kind of decision, and of how to make such decisions deliberately, knowing what each one gives up.

The subject has a reputation for diagrams and vocabulary, yet most of its questions can be settled with arithmetic and a careful look at code. Counting the links between two modules tells you how far a change in one will spread, multiplying the availabilities of the services in a chain tells you how often the chain will fail, and asking how many programs read a field tells you what renaming it will cost. Every principle and pattern you meet here is judged in the same way, by what it costs and what it buys in a system you can see.
outcomes: You'll be able to name the decisions that are architectural and state a quality attribute as a testable scenario.
You'll be able to count the dependencies between modules and recognise coupling, cohesion and the smells that show a misplaced boundary.
You'll be able to apply design principles and patterns, and say where each one stops helping.
You'll be able to model a domain with entities, value objects, aggregates and bounded contexts.
You'll be able to design code so that it can be tested without its dependencies, and check which way its dependencies point.
You'll be able to weigh a modular monolith against microservices, classify a change to a contract, and record a decision.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on How Computers Solve Problems, Python for Data Analysis.

modules.title: Why structure matters
modules.description: What architecture decides, and the ideas of coupling, cohesion, hiding and principles that make code cheap to change.

modules.title: Building blocks of a design
modules.description: Composition, patterns, domain models and testability, shown in small runnable code.

modules.title: Architecture styles
modules.description: Layers and ports, monolith and microservices, events, and contracts that can evolve.

modules.title: Communicating and evolving
modules.description: Diagrams, decision records, weighing trade-offs and changing a running system safely.

concepts.title: Architecture
concepts.summary: The set of decisions about structure that are costly to change later.

concepts.title: Quality attribute
concepts.summary: A property such as performance, security or modifiability that the system must have and that often conflicts with another.

concepts.title: Quality attribute scenario
concepts.summary: A requirement written as source, stimulus, artefact, environment, response and response measure, so that it can be tested.

concepts.title: Reversibility
concepts.summary: How much it costs to undo a decision, which tells you how much care it deserves.

concepts.title: Coupling
concepts.summary: How much one module must know about, or change with, another.

concepts.title: Cohesion
concepts.summary: How closely the parts of a module belong together; a cohesive module has one purpose.

concepts.title: Dependency count
concepts.summary: If every one of n modules depends on every other, there are n(n-1)/2 pairs, so 10 modules have 45.

concepts.title: Change smells
concepts.summary: Shotgun surgery means one change edits many modules, and feature envy means a method uses another class's data more than its own.

concepts.title: Information hiding
concepts.summary: Each module conceals one design decision that may change, behind an interface that does not reveal it.

concepts.title: Interface
concepts.summary: What callers may rely on; everything else is implementation and may change.

concepts.title: Leaky abstraction
concepts.summary: An interface that exposes an implementation detail, so callers come to depend on it.

concepts.title: Single responsibility
concepts.summary: A module should have one reason to change.

concepts.title: Liskov substitution
concepts.summary: Code that works with a base type must keep working when given a subtype, which means the subtype must honour the base type's behaviour.

concepts.title: Dependency inversion
concepts.summary: High-level code depends on an abstraction that it owns, and low-level code implements that abstraction.

concepts.title: YAGNI and DRY
concepts.summary: Do not build for needs you do not have, and do not duplicate knowledge, remembering that code that merely looks alike is not always the same knowledge.

concepts.title: Polymorphism
concepts.summary: Calling the same method on different objects and having each do its own work.

concepts.title: Composition
concepts.summary: Building behaviour by holding other objects and delegating to them.

concepts.title: Subclass explosion
concepts.summary: With 3 transports and 3 payload formats, inheritance needs 9 classes, composition needs 3 + 3 = 6.

concepts.title: Design pattern
concepts.summary: A named, reusable solution to a recurring design problem, with its trade-offs.

concepts.title: Observer
concepts.summary: A subject notifies subscribers of change without knowing what they do.

concepts.title: Strategy and adapter
concepts.summary: A strategy swaps an algorithm behind one interface, and an adapter makes one interface look like another.

concepts.title: Pattern misuse
concepts.summary: Applying a pattern before the problem appears adds indirection without benefit.

concepts.title: Ubiquitous language
concepts.summary: One vocabulary shared by developers and domain experts, used in the conversation and in the code.

concepts.title: Entity and value object
concepts.summary: An entity is identified by an identity that persists as its data changes, and a value object is defined entirely by its data.

concepts.title: Aggregate
concepts.summary: A cluster of objects changed together through one root, which protects an invariant such as 'an order's lines sum to its total'.

concepts.title: Bounded context
concepts.summary: A boundary within which a term has one meaning, since 'customer' may mean different things in sales and in shipping.

concepts.title: Seam
concepts.summary: A place where behaviour can be replaced without editing the code, such as an argument that supplies a dependency.

concepts.title: Test double
concepts.summary: A stand-in for a dependency: a stub returns canned answers, a fake has a working simple implementation and a mock records calls to check them.

concepts.title: Pure function
concepts.summary: A function whose result depends only on its arguments and which changes nothing else, so it needs no setup.

concepts.title: Test pyramid
concepts.summary: Many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests and few end-to-end tests.

concepts.title: Layered architecture
concepts.summary: Code is grouped into layers such as presentation, application, domain and data, each depending only on the layer below.

concepts.title: Ports and adapters
concepts.summary: The domain defines ports, which are the interfaces it needs and offers, and adapters connect them to databases, web frameworks and other systems.

concepts.title: Dependency rule
concepts.summary: Source-code dependencies point inward, toward the domain, never outward to frameworks.

concepts.title: Modular monolith
concepts.summary: One deployable unit whose code is divided into modules with enforced boundaries.

concepts.title: Microservices
concepts.summary: Independently deployable services, each owning its data and communicating over the network.

concepts.title: Conway's law
concepts.summary: A system's structure tends to mirror the communication structure of the organisation that builds it.

concepts.title: Cost of distribution
concepts.summary: Every call that crosses the network can fail or be slow, and availability multiplies: five 99.9% services in a chain give about 99.5%.

concepts.title: Command and event
concepts.summary: A command asks for something to happen and may be refused, and an event records that something happened and cannot be.

concepts.title: Choreography and orchestration
concepts.summary: In choreography each service reacts to events; in orchestration a coordinator tells each service what to do.

concepts.title: Event sourcing
concepts.summary: State is stored as the sequence of events and rebuilt by replaying them.

concepts.title: CQRS
concepts.summary: Separating the model that changes data (commands) from the model that reads it (queries).

concepts.title: Contract
concepts.summary: What a provider promises and a consumer relies on: fields, types, meaning, errors and limits.

concepts.title: Breaking change
concepts.summary: A change that makes a correct existing client fail: removing or renaming a field, changing a type, or tightening validation.

concepts.title: Tolerant reader
concepts.summary: A consumer that ignores fields it does not know and defaults ones that are missing.

concepts.title: Expand then contract
concepts.summary: Add the new form alongside the old, move clients across, then remove the old.

concepts.title: C4 levels
concepts.summary: Context, containers, components and code: four zoom levels, each answering a different question for a different audience.

concepts.title: Container
concepts.summary: A separately runnable unit such as a web application, a mobile app or a database; it is not a Docker container.

concepts.title: Diagram hygiene
concepts.summary: Every element has a name, a type and a short description, every arrow says what it carries, and a key explains shapes and colours.

concepts.title: Trade-off analysis
concepts.summary: Comparing options against the quality attributes that matter, with weights that reflect the requirements.

concepts.title: Architecture decision record
concepts.summary: A short document of one decision: title, status, context, decision and consequences.

concepts.title: Fitness function
concepts.summary: An automated check that a chosen property still holds, such as 'no module in domain imports the web framework'.

concepts.title: Technical debt
concepts.summary: A shortcut taken to deliver sooner, which accrues interest as every later change costs more until it is repaid.

concepts.title: Strangler fig pattern
concepts.summary: Route requests to new code piece by piece until the old system has no work left and can be removed.

concepts.title: Instability
concepts.summary: I = Ce / (Ca + Ce), where Ce counts outgoing dependencies and Ca incoming ones; a module with many dependents should be stable.

concepts.title: Refactoring
concepts.summary: Changing structure without changing behaviour, protected by tests.

lessons.title: What architecture decides

reveal.text: Every reader had the old name written into its own code, which is what makes a public name expensive.

steps.headline: Architecture is the set of decisions that are costly to change later.

lead.text: Renaming tmp costs one edit, because only its own function uses the name, and renaming cust costs thirteen, because twelve other programs use it too, although the two edits are the same size. What separates the two cases is how many other things have come to depend on the decision, and that is the property which makes a decision **architectural**. Choosing the name of a local variable is a design decision, but it is a small one, because nothing outside the function knows the name. Choosing the shape of a public data format is architectural, because every client copies it into its own code.

The figure places four decisions on a line from cheap to costly to change. Use the second view to see what happens to one of them as clients arrive: the shape of the API starts in the middle of the line, where changing it still affects only its author, and moves to the costly end once other programs read it.

afterFigure.text: It follows that architecture is not the diagram. A diagram records decisions, and a box-and-arrow picture of a system drawn on a whiteboard changes nothing about its cost of change. What *does* is the decision itself, such as which data a service exposes, which modules may call which, and how services share a database. Throughout this course we ask the same question of any proposed change: how many other things will have to move if this is wrong?

reveal.text: The same test applies to a database engine or a message format: the more programs depend on the choice, the further right it sits on the line.

steps.headline: A quality attribute is a property the system must have, and the properties often conflict.

lead.text: Decisions are judged by the properties they give the system. These are called **quality attributes**: performance, availability, security, modifiability, testability, and the others in the ISO/IEC 25010 list, whose first edition appeared in 2011 and which was revised in 2023. A requirement such as "the shop must let customers pay" says what the system does; a quality attribute says how well it does it.

The attributes cannot all be maximised together, because the means of getting one often costs another. The figure shows the commonest example. Encrypting every message between a client and a service makes the message unreadable in transit, which improves security, but the encrypt and decrypt steps add work to every message, so latency rises.

afterFigure.text: A good architecture therefore does not maximise every quality. It chooses which qualities matter most for this system, accepts a cost in the others, and records the choice. A payments service might pay the latency of encryption without a second thought, while a live-video relay might not.

diagram.alt: Two versions of a message from a client to a service. In the first it is sent as it is. In the second it is encrypted before sending and decrypted on arrival, which adds two steps.
diagram.caption: Encryption buys security and costs time on every message. Use the buttons to compare.

reveal.text: Availability, testability and modifiability each trade against others in the same way, and the later lessons meet several of these conflicts.

steps.headline: A quality attribute scenario states a requirement in six parts, and the last part makes it testable.

lead.text: The requirement that a checkout "should be fast" cannot be tested, because nothing says how fast, for whom or under what load. A **quality attribute scenario** repairs this by writing the requirement in six parts: the *source* that starts it, the *stimulus* that arrives, the *artefact* of the system that is hit, the *environment* at the time, the *response* the system gives, and the **response measure**, which is the number that a test compares with the result.

The second view of the figure fills the parts in for a checkout. A customer is the source, 1,000 simultaneous orders are the stimulus, the checkout is the artefact, normal operation is the environment, accepting the orders is the response, and 99% within 2 seconds is the measure.

afterFigure.text: Because the measure is a number, the scenario can fail. If 985 of 1,000 orders are accepted within 2 seconds, the system has missed it, and the team can then weigh the cost of fixing that against what the other qualities need. "It should be fast" allows neither a failing test nor a trade.

lead.text: The scenario has six labelled parts, and only one of them holds the number that a test checks.

reveal.text: Each of the six parts can be changed independently, so one system usually has several scenarios for the same quality.

steps.headline: Turn "login should stay available" into a scenario.

workedSteps.text: A requirement without a number cannot be tested, so start by naming the six parts. The event is a user attempting to log in, so the source is a user and the stimulus is a login request.
workedSteps.math: Source: a user. Stimulus: a login request.

workedSteps.text: The part of the system that receives it is the authentication service, and the condition we care about is that one of its two servers has failed.
workedSteps.math: Artefact: the authentication service. Environment: one of two servers down.

workedSteps.text: The system should still let the user in, so the response is that the other server serves the request, and the measure is that 99.9% of 10,000 requests succeed. Work out how many may fail.

steps.headline: Complete a scenario for the checkout under a heavier load.

workedSteps.text: The stimulus is now 5,000 simultaneous orders, and the response and artefact stay as before.
The measure stays 99% within 2 seconds, and the test counts the orders that miss the limit.
The measure allows 1% of 5,000 orders to take longer than 2 seconds. Work out how many.

steps.headline: Reversibility tells you how much care a decision deserves and when it can wait.

lead.text: The cost of changing a decision is its **reversibility**. A decision that is cheap to undo, such as the library behind a function, can be made quickly and corrected when it proves wrong. One that is costly to undo, such as the public API or the way services share data, deserves the early attention and the written reasons, because a wrong choice is paid for later by every program that depends on it.

This also answers a common worry, that an architect must decide everything before any code exists. Only the hard-to-reverse decisions need to be made early, and the cheap ones can wait until the project has shown what is needed. A companion course, System Design, sizes systems for load and failure; this one shapes the code and the boundaries between its parts, and returns to reversibility whenever a boundary is drawn.

A team has three open decisions: the order of import statements in each file, whether two services will share one database, and the name of a private function. They have time to settle only one of them before coding starts.
Decide which deserves the time, using what you have learned about reversal.

reveal.text: Sharing a database ties each service to the other's table layout, so a later change to either has to be agreed with both teams.

lessons.orientation: Name architectural decisions, write a requirement as a six-part scenario, and judge how hard a decision is to reverse.
lessons.nextAction: Count the dependencies between modules and say what makes a boundary good or bad.

blocks.text: Here are two renames of the same size. Inside a billing function, a variable called tmp becomes total, and in the JSON that a customer service sends out, a field called cust becomes customer_id. Each is a change of a few characters in a single file.

The first is finished as soon as it is saved. The second can take weeks, with a new version of the service, a notice to other teams and a period in which both names have to be supported, although the edit itself is no larger. What makes one decision so much dearer to undo than another is the question **software architecture** is built on, and the answer lies in what else has been written on the assumption that the decision will not change.

diagram.caption: The same kind of edit, a rename, costs very different amounts. Use the buttons to compare the two.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to sort decisions by how costly they are to reverse, and to write a requirement as a scenario with a number a test can check.
intro.whyItMatters: Early choices about structure are the ones that cannot be corrected cheaply later.

recap.keyIdea: Architecture is the set of decisions that are costly to change, and a scenario with a measurable response measure is how its qualities are made testable.

blocks.text: The decisions that matter most are those many other things come to depend on, so a public API is architectural while a local name is not. Qualities such as security and latency pull against each other, which is why a requirement is best written as a scenario whose response measure can pass or fail, and why the amount of care should follow the cost of reversing the decision.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson counts the dependencies between modules, which is the measurement behind the question "how many things move if this changes?".

lessons.title: Coupling and cohesion

lead.text: Suppose five modules in a program each need to know about every one of the others, so that each pair has its own link to keep correct.

reveal.text: The first guess is often 5 × 5 or 5 × 4. Both count every link twice or include a module's link to itself.

steps.headline: The number of links between n modules, when all depend on all, is n × (n − 1) ÷ 2.

lead.text: Each module can be linked to the n − 1 others, which gives n × (n − 1) when the count is made from every module's side. A link between two modules has been counted from both of its ends, so dividing by two gives the number of distinct links: **n × (n − 1) ÷ 2**. Four modules therefore have 6 links, six have 15, and ten have 45.

These links are what the word **coupling** measures: how much one module must know about, or change with, another. A link is a place where a change in one module can break the other, so the figure is a count of places where change can spread.

afterFigure.text: The growth is the point. Doubling from ten modules to twenty does not double the number of links, it takes it from 45 to 190, because every new module can link to all the old ones. A hub arrangement avoids this: ten modules around one hub need 9 links, and twenty need 19. Zero links is not the aim, since modules must communicate. The aim is that the links which exist are few and deliberate.

diagram.alt: A bar chart of links when every module depends on every other. Four modules need 6 links, six need 15, ten need 45 and twenty need 190.
diagram.caption: The number of possible links grows much faster than the number of modules.

steps.headline: Coupling comes in kinds, and the tighter the kind, the more a change in one module spreads.

lead.text: Not all links are equally costly. The figure lists five kinds from tight to loose. At the tight end a caller reaches into another module's internals, as when code reads stack._items directly, so any change to the layout of those internals breaks it. Two modules that write one global variable are also tightly bound, because neither can change how it uses the variable without the other noticing.

A **control flag**, an argument such as fast=True that selects what the callee does inside, makes the caller know about the callee's inner paths. Passing plain data, such as a number, requires the caller to know only the meaning of that value, and sending a message, such as an event, requires only that both agree on the message.

afterFigure.text: The rule of thumb is to move links down the ladder where you can. Replacing a read of stack._items with a call to a function that returns the length turns shared internals into passed data, and the stack is then free to change what it stores.

diagram.alt: Five kinds of coupling listed from tightest to loosest: shared internals, shared global data, control flags, passed data and messages, each with a short example.
diagram.caption: Coupling kinds from tight at the top to loose at the bottom.

reveal.text: Passing the value itself, rather than a flag that picks a path, is the looser alternative.

steps.headline: Cohesion is how closely a module's parts belong together, and a cohesive module has one reason to change.

lead.text: Coupling describes the links between modules. **Cohesion** describes what is inside one: a module is cohesive when everything in it serves a single purpose. The figure shows an Invoice class with four methods and the four fields they use, with a dot wherever a method uses a field. Two methods use the invoice's lines and tax rate, and the other two use an address and a mail server's host, so the dots form two separate groups that never share a field.

That separation is a warning. A class that formats invoices and also sends email has two reasons to change, since a new tax rule edits one group and a new mail provider edits the other, and a change made for either reason has to be tested against the other group as well.

afterFigure.text: Splitting the class makes each group a class of its own, and the second view shows the result: every method uses every field of its class. A module called utils usually fails this test in the opposite way. Its parts share only the fact that they are helpful, so it has as many reasons to change as it has functions.

diagram.caption: Dots show which fields each method uses. Use the buttons to compare one class with two.

steps.headline: Follow what the caller of order.customer.address.country depends on.

workedSteps.text: The expression starts at order and reads customer, then address, then country, so the caller walks through objects it did not create.
If Address renames country to country_code, the expression fails, and so does every other caller that wrote the same chain.
Count the classes whose layout this single line relies on, not including the plain value at the end.

steps.headline: Smells show a boundary in the wrong place, and the fix is to move behaviour next to the data it uses.

lead.text: Three smells recur. In **shotgun surgery**, a single change forces edits across many modules, as in the first view, where each of four modules carries its own price formatting. In **feature envy**, a method uses another class's data more than its own, so it sits far from what it works on. In a **god class**, one class collects so many responsibilities that nearly every change touches it.

All three come from behaviour that is far from the data or decision it depends on. The repair is the same each time: move it nearby. The second view shows shotgun surgery repaired by moving the formatting into one money module, which the four modules then call, and a method with feature envy moves onto the class whose fields it reads.

afterFigure.text: After the move the dependency count falls as well, since the four modules now depend on one module and no longer repeat a decision among themselves.

diagram.alt: Before: four modules each contain their own price formatting, so a currency change edits four modules. After: one money module holds the format and the four modules call it.

lead.text: The first view of the figure shows one decision written in four places, and a change to it forces four edits.

reveal.text: The next question gives the opposite problem, one method in the wrong class.

lead.text: A method on Report reads six fields of Customer to build a line of text and reads one of Report's own fields. Moving the method onto Customer would shorten every call it makes.

reveal.text: A method that talks mostly to another class's data is a candidate to move there.

lessons.orientation: Count dependencies between modules, tell cohesive modules from scattered ones, and name the smells that show a misplaced boundary.
lessons.nextAction: Describe how a module hides a decision behind an interface, and why Parnas split a program that way.

blocks.text: Ten modules that all depend on one another have 45 links between them, and each link is a place where a change in one module can break another. The same ten modules arranged around a single hub have 9. Nothing about either program is wrong at first sight, and yet one of them will cost far more to change than the other, because the number of links, rather than the number of modules, sets how far a change can spread.
The figure counts both. The choice of which links to allow is a design decision that gets expensive once code depends on it, so it is a good place to start measuring.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to count the links between modules, recognise a cohesive module, and name the smell when a change is scattered across many places.

recap.keyIdea: Fewer, deliberate links between modules, and modules whose parts all serve one purpose, are what keep a change from spreading.

blocks.text: Linking n modules in all pairs gives n × (n − 1) ÷ 2 links, so the count grows much faster than the modules do, and the aim is to keep the links few and loose rather than to remove them. Cohesion asks the same question inside a module, whether its parts share one purpose, and smells such as shotgun surgery and feature envy show where behaviour has been put far from the data or decision it depends on.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson shows how a module can hide a decision completely, so that callers cannot come to depend on it.

lessons.title: Hiding decisions behind interfaces

lead.text: A small program is built in four steps: read the input, shift each line, sort the lines, and print them. All four steps read the lines from one shared table, so each knows how the table is laid out. A fifth module is added that also reads the table.

reveal.text: This is the situation David Parnas set against a different way of splitting the program in 1972.

steps.headline: Modules are best chosen by the design decision each one hides, rather than by the steps of the program.

lead.text: In his paper of December 1972, David Parnas compared two ways of splitting a small program that builds a keyword-in-context index. The first split follows the order of processing: one module to read the input, one to shift the lines, one to sort them, and one to print. The second gives each module one design decision that was likely to change, and the most important of these was how lines are stored.

The figure shows what a change to the storage format does under each split. When the modules follow the steps, every one of them reads the stored lines itself, so the format is known to all of them and all of them change together. When one module owns the format and the rest ask it for lines, only that module changes.

afterFigure.text: Parnas's criterion, now called **information hiding**, is therefore a rule for drawing boundaries: put a decision that is difficult or likely to change inside a module, and let the module's **interface** tell callers only what they may rely on. Modules shaped by steps look natural on a flowchart, but a flowchart is the *wrong* thing to optimise, since it shows the order of events and not the decisions that will change.

diagram.alt: Two ways to split the same four-step program. When modules follow the processing steps, all four know the line storage format and all change when it does. When one module hides the storage format, only that module changes.
diagram.caption: A change to how lines are stored, under two ways of splitting the program. Use the buttons to compare.

steps.headline: An interface is what callers may rely on, and everything behind it may change.

lead.text: A stack gives the idea in its smallest form. Its interface is two operations, push, which adds an item, and pop, which removes the item added most recently. The figure shows the version used in this lesson, whose items are held in a Python list, and the second view shows the same interface with a different structure inside. The caller, drawn above the box, is identical in both views, because it uses only the interface.

The structure holding the items is the stack's hidden decision. Because callers have only push and pop to work with, the author can replace the list by anything that behaves the same, for speed or for memory, and no caller needs to be edited. The test of a good interface is exactly this: the author can change what is inside without asking anyone.

diagram.caption: The interface stays the same while the decision inside is swapped. Use the buttons to swap it.

steps.headline: An interface leaks when it exposes a detail, and callers then depend on that detail.

lead.text: Hiding fails when a caller reaches past the interface. Suppose a caller reads stack._items[0], because it is convenient. The code works, and it carries a hidden cost: it now depends on the stack storing its items under that name and in that order. The author can no longer change either without breaking the caller, and the decision that was meant to be hidden has been *shared*. An interface that lets this happen, or a caller that does it, produces a **leaky abstraction**.

Python gives only a convention against it. A name that begins with an underscore signals that it is internal, but the language does not stop other code from reading it, so a stack's hiding is only as strong as its callers' discipline.

afterFigure.text: The second view of the figure shows the consequence. The first caller uses push and pop and survives every change inside the stack. The second depends on _items, so renaming the field, or storing items in a different structure, breaks it on the day the author makes the change, which may be months after the caller was written.

diagram.alt: A caller and a Stack. In the first view the caller uses the interface push and pop. In the second it reaches past the interface to read the hidden field _items, so it breaks if the field is renamed.

lead.text: Think about what the second caller in the figure promised the stack's author, and what the author promised it.

reveal.text: The same reasoning applies to any detail that is reachable, not only to names with underscores.

steps.headline: An interface is more than a list of method names: it includes behaviour such as ordering, errors and performance.

lead.text: Callers rely on more than the names of operations. For the stack, they rely on the *order* in which items come out, newest first. They may rely on what happens when pop is called on an empty stack, which in Python is usually an error rather than a quiet default, and on the stack being fast, so that pop does not take longer when the stack holds more items. All of this is part of the interface, and a change to any of it can break a caller without a single method name changing.

This also tells you what a module should hide. Choose a module for each decision that is likely to change, such as how data is stored, how a message is formatted, or how a price is worked out, and give each an interface that states the behaviour callers may depend on and nothing else.

afterFigure.text: A pricing module is a typical example. Checkout, invoice and report call one discount function, and the rule inside can move from a flat 10% to a tiered rule without any of them being edited.

steps.headline: Change a discount rule that a pricing module hides.

workedSteps.text: Three modules, checkout, invoice and report, each call pricing.discount(total) and use the number returned.
The rule inside pricing changes from a flat 10% of the total to 10% only when the total is above 100. The signature discount(total) stays the same, so no caller sees a difference in how it is called.
Count the modules whose source has to be edited.

lead.text: The stack's author decides that pop on an empty stack should return None instead of raising an error. Every method name stays the same, yet some callers break.

reveal.text: The change was to a promise the interface made, though not one a signature records.

lessons.orientation: Explain what a module hides, what an interface promises, and how a leak makes a hidden decision shared.
lessons.nextAction: Apply design principles such as single responsibility and dependency inversion, and say where they stop helping.

blocks.text: In December 1972 David Parnas published a paper that took a small program and split it into modules twice. The first split followed the order in which the program works, with one module for each step. The second gave each module a decision that might change, such as how lines are stored, and then asked what happens to each split when that decision does change.
The difference between the two shows a rule that is still used for drawing boundaries: a module should be chosen for what it hides, and a caller should know only what the module promises.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say what a module hides, which behaviours belong to its interface, and why a caller that reaches inside makes a hidden decision shared.

recap.keyIdea: A module should hide one decision likely to change, and its interface should promise only what callers may rely on.

blocks.text: Parnas showed that splitting a program by the decisions that might change confines a change to one module, whereas splitting by steps spreads it. An interface covers behaviour such as order, errors and speed as well as names, and a caller that reaches past it, as stack._items[0] does, turns a hidden decision into a shared one.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns this into principles, such as single responsibility and dependency inversion, and asks where each stops being useful.

lessons.title: Principles as heuristics

steps.headline: The SOLID principles are five rules of thumb for deciding where code should depend on what.

lead.text: Robert Martin collected five principles for object-oriented design, and Michael Feathers later made their initials into the word **SOLID**. Each is a short statement about dependency. A class should have one reason to change; behaviour should be added without editing code that works; a subtype should honour what its base type promises; a caller should see only the operations it uses; and high-level code should depend on abstractions that it owns, with low-level code implementing them.

These are **heuristics**, in the sense that they are rules of thumb which usually help and sometimes do harm. Each trades against simplicity, because following every principle everywhere gives a program of many small classes and interfaces, and the cost of that indirection is paid every time somebody reads the code. The rest of the lesson takes two of the principles in detail and then the two warnings, YAGNI and DRY, that keep the others in proportion.

diagram.alt: Five design principles known as SOLID, each with a one-line summary: single responsibility, open-closed, Liskov substitution, interface segregation and dependency inversion.
diagram.caption: The five principles. Treat them as rules of thumb, not laws.

cases.label: The five principles

lead.text: In geometry, a square is a rectangle. A Square class therefore subclasses Rectangle, and, to keep itself square, each of its setters sets both sides. The function stretch takes any rectangle, sets its width to 5 and its height to 2, and returns its area.

reveal.text: A Rectangle(1, 1) gives 10 for the same call, so the two objects disagree about what stretch means.

steps.headline: A subtype must honour what its base type promises, or code written for the base type breaks.

lead.text: The figure follows the same call through the two objects. A Rectangle, given a width of 5 and a height of 2, has an area of 10. A Square given the same two calls ends with both sides equal to 2, so its area is 4. The function stretch was written for Rectangles and relied on the fact that the setters change one side each, and a Square quietly breaks that fact.

This is a violation of the **Liskov substitution principle**, which says that code that works with a base type must keep working when given a subtype. Barbara Liskov introduced the idea in a 1987 keynote and formalised it with Jeannette Wing in 1994. The test is about *behaviour*, not about the shape of the hierarchy: a square is a rectangle in geometry, where figures do not change, but a mutable Square is not a mutable Rectangle, because it promises less about its setters.

afterFigure.text: The practical sign of a violation is a subclass that overrides a method to refuse, weaken or contradict what the base class promised, such as a Penguin whose fly raises an error. The usual repair is to drop the inheritance, and to give the two classes a common smaller interface that does not promise what only one of them can do.

diagram.alt: The same function stretch called with a Rectangle and with a Square. With a Rectangle the area is 5 times 2, which is 10. With a Square both setters change both sides, so the area is 2 times 2, which is 4.
diagram.caption: The same call on two objects gives different areas. Use the buttons to switch the object passed in.

lead.text: Apply the first principle in the list to a class with several jobs.

reveal.text: Splitting such a class is the same move as the Invoice and Mailer split in the lesson on cohesion.

steps.headline: Dependency inversion makes high-level code own the abstraction and lets low-level code implement it.

lead.text: In the first view of the figure, Checkout calls EmailNotifier and SmsNotifier by name. Every new channel means an edit to Checkout, and every change to a notifier is felt there, because the high-level policy of when to notify depends on the low-level detail of how.

**Dependency inversion** reverses that. Checkout defines a small interface, called Notifier here, with one operation, send, which describes what Checkout needs. The email and SMS classes implement it, so in the second view their arrows point *up* at the interface that the high-level code owns. Checkout now calls notifier.send() and neither knows nor cares which channel is behind it.

afterFigure.text: This is the same move as information hiding, seen from the dependency's side. A new Pager channel is added as one more class that implements Notifier, and the existing classes stay unedited.

diagram.alt: Two dependency diagrams. Before, Checkout depends directly on EmailNotifier and SmsNotifier. After, Checkout depends on a Notifier abstraction that it owns, and both notifiers implement it, so the arrows from the low-level code now point upward.
diagram.caption: Checkout before and after depending on an abstraction. Use the buttons to compare.

steps.headline: Add a channel to a checkout that depends on an abstraction.

workedSteps.text: Checkout holds a Notifier and calls notifier.send(message) when an order is placed. EmailNotifier and SmsNotifier both implement send.
A Pager notifier is written with its own send method, and the program passes a Pager to Checkout at start-up.
Count the existing classes whose source has to change.

steps.headline: YAGNI and DRY keep the principles in proportion, and look-alike code is not always the same knowledge.

lead.text: Every principle so far adds structure, so two warnings balance them. **YAGNI**, short for "you aren't gonna need it", says not to build for a need you do not have yet, because the guess is often wrong and the unused abstraction still has to be read and kept. **DRY**, "don't repeat yourself", says that each piece of *knowledge* should live in one place, so that a change is made once.

The two meet in the rule of three: leave a repetition alone the first time it appears, tolerate it the second, and write the abstraction when it appears a third time, because by then you can see what the copies really share. The figure shows why waiting helps. Two date-formatting functions look alike, but one serves invoices, whose format follows tax law, and the other serves logs, whose format follows tooling. Merged, they change for two reasons, and a change for one would risk the other.

diagram.alt: Two date-formatting functions that look alike. Merged, one function serves invoices, which change with tax law, and logs, which change with tooling. Kept apart, each changes for one reason.
diagram.caption: Code that looks alike may not be the same knowledge. Use the buttons to compare.

lead.text: Use the rule of three on a repetition that has appeared twice.

reveal.text: The same rule applies to a class hierarchy, an interface, or a configuration option.

lead.text: A base class Bird has the method fly. A new subclass Penguin overrides fly so that it raises an error, because penguins cannot fly. A function that loops over a list of Birds and calls fly on each one now crashes when the list contains a Penguin.

reveal.text: Dropping the inheritance and giving Bird a smaller interface that does not promise flight is one repair.

lessons.orientation: Apply single responsibility, Liskov substitution and dependency inversion, and say when YAGNI and DRY argue against more structure.
lessons.nextAction: Use composition and polymorphism instead of deep inheritance, and count the classes that each approach needs.

blocks.text: Here is a function that sets a rectangle's width to 5 and its height to 2 and returns its area. Given a Rectangle that starts at 1 by 1, it returns 10. Given a Square, which is a rectangle in geometry and a subclass of Rectangle in code, it returns something else, because a Square cannot hold a width and a height that differ.

The function was correct, the subclass was defensible, and the program is still wrong. Cases like this are why design principles exist, and also why they are best read as rules of thumb that predict where trouble will arise, not as laws that settle every question.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to spot a Liskov violation, show how dependency inversion changes the direction of an arrow, and say when a principle would add more structure than it saves.

recap.keyIdea: The SOLID principles are rules of thumb about dependency, and YAGNI and DRY limit how far to apply them.

blocks.text: A subtype has to honour what its base type promises, as the Square fails to when its setters change both sides, and high-level code is easier to change when it owns the abstraction that low-level code implements. Because each principle adds structure, YAGNI and the rule of three say to wait until repetition shows what is shared, since code that looks alike may change for different reasons.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at composition and polymorphism, and at how inheritance can multiply classes where composition does not.

lessons.title: Composition and polymorphism

lead.text: Two classes each have a method called area. A list holds one object of each, and a loop calls area on every item and adds up the results.

reveal.text: The loop contains no test for the kind of object, and it works.

diagram.alt: Python code defining Rect and Tri, each with an area method, and a print of the sum of the areas of a list holding Rect(2, 3) and Tri(4, 5).

steps.headline: Polymorphism means one call is answered differently by each object, and each object supplies its own answer.

lead.text: The figure follows the loop in the program. The call s.area() is written once. For the first item it runs the method defined on Rect, which multiplies width by height, and for the second it runs the method defined on Tri, which takes half the base times the height. The loop never asks what kind of object it holds, so a new kind of shape can be added without editing the loop. This is **polymorphism**: the same call, answered by each object in its own way.

In many languages polymorphism is tied to inheritance, since the loop would be typed as holding some parent class. Python is looser. A call such as s.area() looks the method up on the object at the moment of the call, so any object that has the method will do, whatever class it came from. This is often called duck typing, and the standard library's typing.Protocol lets a program describe the methods it expects without forcing a parent class.

afterFigure.text: It follows that inheritance is not what makes the loop work. It is one way of promising that every object has the method, and the previous lesson showed what it costs when the promise is broken.

lead.text: Follow the argument in the last paragraph on a class that shares no parent with the others.

reveal.text: The method is found by name on the object, not by checking its ancestry.

lead.text: A notifier has to send over three transports, email, SMS and push, and in three formats, plain text, JSON and XML. A developer writes one subclass of Sender for each combination, such as EmailJsonSender.

reveal.text: The two choices vary independently, which is what makes the count grow.

steps.headline: Inheritance multiplies classes when two things vary independently, and composition adds them.

lead.text: The count in the last question is a product. Each new transport needs a subclass for every format, and each new format needs one for every transport, so the number of classes is 3 × 3 = 9 now and grows as the lists do. With four transports and five formats it would be 20. This growth is called a **combinatorial explosion**, and it is the usual sign that a hierarchy is trying to hold two independent choices in one tree.

**Composition** builds behaviour by holding other objects and delegating to them. A Sender holds a transport and a formatter, and each is a small class of its own, so the figure shows three transport classes and three format classes, six in all, and the pair is chosen when the Sender is built. A new transport adds one class and no more, since it works with every existing format at once.

afterFigure.text: The saving also changes what a test needs. A Sender that takes any object with a send method can be given a fake that records its messages, and no real network is involved.

steps.headline: Inherit for substitutable specialisation, and compose to reuse behaviour.

lead.text: A sentence in English does not prove that inheritance will work in code. "A square is a rectangle" is true in geometry, and the last lesson showed that a mutable Square cannot stand in for a mutable Rectangle. The working test is substitution: inherit when every use of the parent can safely take the child, and compose when you only want to use what another class does.

Reuse is the more common need, and for it composition is the safer choice, since a class that holds another is not bound by its methods or by its future changes. Some frameworks do ask for inheritance, by requiring a class to extend one of theirs, and in that case the rule bends: inherit where the framework needs it, and keep the rest of the design in smaller composed parts that do not depend on the framework.
A team tests its Sender by handing it a small fake object that has a send method and records what it is given. The fake does not inherit from the real transport class.

reveal.text: This is what allows the Sender to be tested without a real transport.

lessons.orientation: Trace a polymorphic call through a list, and choose between inheritance and composition by counting the classes each needs.
lessons.nextAction: Name the patterns that solve common design problems, and refuse the ones that have no problem to solve.

blocks.text: The expression sum(s.area() for s in [Rect(2, 3), Tri(4, 5)]) adds a rectangle's area and a triangle's, and it contains no test for which is which. Each object answers the same call in its own way, which is why the loop never has to change when a third kind of shape is added.

Inheritance is the first thing many programmers reach for to arrange this, and it does work, but at a price that shows up once two things vary at the same time. That price can be counted and compared with the alternative, which is to build a behaviour out of smaller objects.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to trace a call through objects of different classes and count the classes that inheritance and composition each need.

recap.keyIdea: One call can be answered by many kinds of object, and holding objects often needs fewer classes than inheriting from them.

blocks.text: Polymorphism lets a single call, such as s.area(), run each object's own method, and in Python it needs only that each object has the method. When two choices vary independently, inheritance needs a subclass for each pair, 3 × 3 = 9 here, where composition needs 3 + 3 = 6 parts and lets any pair be chosen at run time.

lessons.title: Patterns that earn their place

steps.headline: A design pattern is a named solution to a recurring problem, and its value is in the problem it names.

lead.text: A **design pattern** is a named, reusable solution to a design problem that keeps appearing, with an account of its trade-offs. The idea came from architecture, where Christopher Alexander's *A Pattern Language* of 1977 set out solutions to recurring problems in buildings. Ward Cunningham and Kent Beck proposed patterns for programming in 1987, and the book *Design Patterns* by Gamma, Helm, Johnson and Vlissides, published in 1994, described 23 of them for object-oriented code.

The figure lists four of the most useful, each with the problem it answers. The name is only a label for the problem, and the label is useful because it lets a team say "this is an observer" in place of describing a half-page of structure. A pattern applied where its problem does not exist is a cost with no benefit, so the aim is to learn the problems and to recognise them when they arise.

afterFigure.text: Patterns are also not tied to classes. Python has first-class functions, so several patterns that need a class in other languages become a function passed as an argument.

diagram.alt: Four design patterns, each paired with the problem it solves: observer, strategy, adapter and factory.
diagram.caption: Each pattern is named for the problem it answers.

steps.headline: An observer pattern lets a subject notify subscribers without knowing what they do.

lead.text: The code in the last question is the **observer** pattern in its smallest form. The subject keeps a list of subscribers and, when something happens, calls each in order. It knows only that each can be called, and not what it does, so a subscriber can log the event, update a screen or send a message, and none of that is the subject's business.

The figure shows both halves. In the first view two functions, f and g, are attached, and in the second notify(5) calls f and then g. The log receives 10 and then 6. The value of the arrangement is in what does *not* need to change: a third subscriber can be attached without editing the subject, and a subscriber can be removed without the subject noticing.

afterFigure.text: The problem it names is therefore a dependency running the wrong way. An order that sent its own emails and updated its own report would depend on both, while an order that merely announces its change depends on neither.

diagram.alt: A Subject holding two subscriber functions. In the first view they are attached. In the second, notify(5) calls the first, which adds 10 to the log, and then the second, which adds 6.
diagram.caption: The subject calls each subscriber in the order they were attached. Use the buttons to switch.

steps.headline: A strategy swaps an algorithm behind one call, and an adapter makes one interface look like another.

lead.text: Sorting with a key function is a **strategy**. The call sorted(words, key=len) always sorts, and the key argument decides how, so passing a different function gives a different order without a change to sorted. Where other languages write a class for each algorithm, Python passes the function itself, and that is the whole pattern.

An **adapter** is for a mismatch between two interfaces. A payment provider's library offers charge_card(cents), while the application's own code was written to call pay(amount) in pounds. The adapter implements pay and calls charge_card inside, multiplying by 100. The application keeps one interface, and if the provider changes, only the adapter is edited.

diagram.alt: Two patterns. A strategy is a function passed in to change behaviour, as the key function len changes how sorted orders words. An adapter turns the application's pay(amount) call into a provider's charge_card(cents) call.
diagram.caption: A strategy swaps behaviour, and an adapter converts an interface. Use the buttons to compare.

The first subscriber appends 6 and the second appends 4, so the log is [6, 4].

steps.headline: A factory chooses the class in one place, and a pattern with no problem to solve only adds indirection.

lead.text: The fourth pattern in the figure, the **factory**, puts the decision about which class to create in one function. Callers ask the factory for a notifier of a given kind and never name the concrete classes, so adding a kind means editing the factory and nothing else. The value is the same as in the other patterns: one decision lives in one place.

The same test shows when not to use a pattern. An interface with one implementation and one caller solves no problem, since nothing varies, and every reader must follow an extra step to find the code that runs. The usual advice follows YAGNI: write the plain code first, and introduce the pattern when a second case arrives and the problem becomes real.

afterFigure.text: A pattern is therefore a response to a problem you can point to, such as two implementations, a mismatched interface or a dependency running the wrong way.

lead.text: A team has one email notifier and one place that sends messages. A developer wants to add a Notifier interface, a factory and an observer list now, in case other channels are wanted later.

reveal.text: The same reasoning applies to configuration options and class hierarchies.

lessons.orientation: Recognise observer, strategy, adapter and factory by the problem each solves, and say when no pattern is needed.
lessons.nextAction: Model a business domain with entities, value objects and bounded contexts.

blocks.text: Python's built-in sorted takes a function as its key, so sorted(['pear', 'fig', 'banana'], key=len) gives ['fig', 'pear', 'banana']. The function passed in changes how the list is ordered without any change to sorted, and programmers have a name for that arrangement: a strategy.

A name of this kind is the point of a design pattern. It records a solution that has worked on a recurring problem, along with the cost, so that a team can use one word where it would otherwise describe a page of structure. Four such patterns can be taken by the problems they solve.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to trace an observer, pair a pattern with its problem, and recognise when a pattern would only add indirection.

recap.keyIdea: A pattern is a named solution to a recurring problem, and it earns its place only when that problem is present.

blocks.text: Observer, strategy, adapter and factory each answer a problem, which is many parts reacting to one change, swapping an algorithm, mismatched interfaces and where to create objects. The pattern's name carries no value on its own, so an interface with one implementation and one caller is indirection without a problem to solve.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns from code to the business domain, and asks how its words and boundaries should shape the model.

lessons.title: Domain modelling

steps.headline: A model starts from the words the business uses, and the code should use the same words.

lead.text: A model of a shop begins with what people there say: an order has lines, a shipment leaves when an order is ready, and a refund returns money for a line. These words are the domain's own, and the code is easier to read and to correct when it uses them. A **ubiquitous language** is one vocabulary, shared by the developers and the domain experts, and used both in conversation and in the code.

The figure shows why it matters. When the code calls an order tbl_ord_hdr, every conversation needs a translation, and a mistake in one translation becomes a defect that nobody can see. When the class is called Order, a domain expert can read the names and say that a refund belongs to a line, not to the whole order.

afterFigure.text: This also gives a check on any code, including code written by a tool: do the names match the words the business uses? A model that cannot be discussed in those words is probably wrong in more than its names.

diagram.alt: Words the business uses (order, refund, shipment) linked to names in the code. In one view the code uses the same words: Order, Refund, Shipment. In the other it uses abbreviations such as tbl_ord_hdr that need translating.
diagram.caption: The same three concepts, named two ways in the code. Use the buttons to compare.

steps.headline: A value object is defined by its data, and an entity is defined by an identity that persists as its data changes.

lead.text: Some things in a domain are interchangeable. Five pounds in one purse is as good as five pounds in another, and two Money objects with the same amount and currency are simply equal. Such a thing is a **value object**: it is defined entirely by its data, it does not change, and a different amount is a different value. A frozen dataclass makes this exact, and the result in the last question follows from it.

Other things must be told apart even when their data is identical. Two orders with the same lines are still two orders, since the customer placed both and will be charged for both. An **entity** is identified by an identity, here an order id, that persists as its data changes: an order can gain a line and be paid and shipped, and remain the same order.

afterFigure.text: The test is therefore to ask whether you would care *which* one you have. If you would, as with an order, a customer or an account, it is an entity and needs an id. If any equal one will do, as with an amount of money, a date range or an address written on a label, it is a value.

diagram.alt: Value objects compared with entities. Two Money objects with the same amount and currency are equal, and a different currency makes a different value. Two orders with identical lines but different ids are two different entities.
diagram.caption: A value is its data, and an entity is its identity. Use the buttons to compare.

steps.headline: An aggregate is a cluster changed only through one root, which keeps an invariant true.

lead.text: Some facts must always hold. An order's total must equal the sum of its lines, and a rule of this kind is called an **invariant**. If any code can change a line directly, the invariant can be broken by code that never meant to break it. An **aggregate** prevents this by making one object, the root, the only way in. Callers do not edit lines; they ask the Order to add one, and the Order changes the lines and the total together.

The figure shows both routes. Through the root, add_line updates the lines and the total in one method, so they cannot disagree. Directly to a line, the total is left stale. The stronger the invariant, the more the root has to guard it, and the fewer places there are to look when it fails.

diagram.alt: An Order aggregate with a root and two lines, 500 times 2 and 300 times 1, and a total of 1300. In one view a caller adds a line through the root and the total stays correct. In the other it edits a line directly and the total is stale.
diagram.caption: Changes through the root keep the invariant. Use the buttons to compare.

steps.headline: A bounded context is a boundary inside which a term has one meaning, and each context keeps its own model.

lead.text: A word in a large business rarely means one thing. In sales a customer is a buyer with a credit limit and an order history. In shipping it is a name, a delivery address and a phone number, and in billing it is a payer with a VAT number. A single Customer class meant to serve all three grows every field and every rule, and a change for one context risks the other two.

A **bounded context** draws a line around the place where a term has one meaning, and gives each such place its own model. The figure shows three, and the same word has three shapes. The contexts do not share a class. They agree only on what passes between them, such as a customer id on an order that leaves sales for shipping.

afterFigure.text: A model is not the database schema either. How a context stores its data is a separate decision, and the model should be written for how the domain is understood and not for how its rows are laid out.

diagram.alt: Three contexts, each with its own Customer. In sales a customer has a name and a credit limit. In shipping it has a delivery address and a phone number. In billing it has a VAT number and a billing address.

lead.text: Take the three views of the figure, and name what each of them is.

reveal.text: Where two contexts meet, the usual practice is to translate between them rather than share a class.

lead.text: In a frozen dataclass, assigning to a field after the object has been created is not allowed. A caller, believing it has a Money of 5 pounds, tries to turn it into 6 pounds by assigning to its amount.

reveal.text: The caller should create a new Money(6, 'GBP') instead.

lessons.orientation: Model a domain with its own words, tell entities from value objects, and place the boundaries where a term changes meaning.
lessons.nextAction: Design code that can be tested without its dependencies, using seams and test doubles.

blocks.text: Three people in one company use the word customer. In sales it means a buyer with a credit limit, in shipping a name and a delivery address, and in billing a payer with a VAT number. The word is the same and the things are different, and a program that treats them as one object will carry the fields and rules of all three.

Domain modelling begins from this observation: before choosing classes, find the words the business uses and what each of them means where it is used. Eric Evans gave the method its name in his 2003 book, Domain-Driven Design, and four of its ideas matter here.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to tell an entity from a value object, explain what an aggregate protects, and say why one word may need several models.

recap.keyIdea: A model uses the business's own words, separates entities from values, guards its invariants through a root, and keeps one model for each context.

blocks.text: A value object is defined by its data and an entity by an identity that persists, and an aggregate lets only its root change the cluster, so that an invariant such as an order's total always holds. Because a word such as customer means different things in sales, shipping and billing, each bounded context keeps its own model.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at design for testing, and at how seams and test doubles let code be tested without its dependencies.

lessons.title: Designing for testability

steps.headline: Code is hard to test when it reaches for its dependencies itself, and the fix is a design change.

lead.text: A function that reads the clock, writes to a database and sends an email is hard to test, and the difficulty is in the design, not in the test tool. The function chooses its own dependencies, so a test cannot choose different ones. It also cannot be run on 29 February, cannot be run without a database, and cannot be run without sending a real email, and each of those is a reason for the test to be slow, flaky or never written.

The figure shows the function with its three dependencies. A **seam** is a place where behaviour can be replaced without editing the code, and the simplest seam is an argument. If the function is *given* its clock, its repository and its mailer, a test can give it fakes, as in the second view, and nothing real is touched.

afterFigure.text: This is the dependency inversion of the earlier lesson, seen from the test's side: the code names what it needs, and the caller decides what to supply.

diagram.alt: A function register drawn with three dependencies plugged into it: the clock, a database and email. In one view they are the real services. In the other each is replaced by a fake, so the function can be tested quickly and repeatably.
diagram.caption: The same code under test with real and with fake dependencies. Use the buttons to swap.

steps.headline: A test double is a stand-in for a dependency, and the three kinds differ in what they do.

lead.text: The class in the last question is one kind of **test double**, which is any stand-in used in a test in place of a real dependency. A **stub** returns canned answers, for a test in which the code under test needs a value from its dependency and nothing more. A **fake** has a simple but working implementation, such as a repository that keeps its records in a list, so that it behaves like the real one in small. A **mock** records the calls it receives, so the test can check afterwards that the right call was made.

Choose the simplest double that serves. A test that replaces everything with mocks ends up testing the mocks, because it checks that the code calls what the test expected it to call, and not what the code achieves. A fake or a stub lets the test check results, which is what a caller cares about.

diagram.alt: Three kinds of test double: a stub returns canned answers, a fake has a simple working implementation, and a mock records the calls it receives.
diagram.caption: Three kinds of stand-in for a dependency.

reveal.text: Writing a real in-memory fake takes a few lines and can be shared across tests.

steps.headline: A pure function needs no doubles, so separating decisions from effects leaves little to fake.

lead.text: A **pure function** is one whose result depends only on its arguments and which changes nothing else. is_adult(age), which returns age >= 18, is pure, and testing it needs no setup, no fake and no cleanup: call it with a value and compare the result. Most of a program's decisions, such as who qualifies, what a total is and which discount applies, can be written this way.

The effects, such as reading the clock, saving and sending, then sit in a thin shell around the pure core. The shell gets its dependencies as arguments and passes values to the core. Nearly all the tests are quick tests of the core, and a few tests with fakes cover the shell.

afterFigure.text: Because a boundary is where a decision changes, the tests that matter most for a pure function sit on its boundaries. For age >= 18 these are 17, which is refused, and 18, which is accepted.

steps.headline: Choose the test cases for the rule age >= 18.

workedSteps.text: The rule changes its answer between two neighbouring ages. Below the limit is 17 and at the limit is 18.
A rule wrongly written as age > 18 would refuse 18, so the case at the limit is the one that catches it.
Count the cases needed at the boundary itself.

steps.headline: The test pyramid puts many fast unit tests at the base and few slow end-to-end tests at the top.

lead.text: Tests differ in what they cover and in what they cost. A unit test runs one function or class with its dependencies faked, so it is fast and points at the fault. An integration test runs several parts together, perhaps against a real database. An end-to-end test drives the whole system, so it is the slowest and the one most likely to fail for reasons unrelated to the change.

The **test pyramid** is the rule of keeping many tests at the base and few at the top. The figure gives an example suite of 200 unit tests, 20 integration tests and 5 end-to-end tests. A design with seams makes the base cheap to build, and a design without them pushes every test up the pyramid, where each is slow.

afterFigure.text: A coverage percentage does not say which layer a test sits in, or whether it checks a result. A suite can touch every line and still check nothing, so coverage is a way to find untested code and no proof that the tests are good.

diagram.alt: A test pyramid with three layers. At the top, 5 end-to-end tests of 20 seconds each. In the middle, 20 integration tests of half a second each. At the base, 200 unit tests of 0.01 seconds each.
diagram.caption: Many fast tests at the base and few slow ones at the top.

lead.text: A function is_leap_day() returns True on 29 February, and it works out the date by reading the system clock inside its body. It can be tested only on the right day, which comes once every four years.

reveal.text: The same change makes any time-dependent code testable.

lessons.orientation: Place seams so that code can be tested without its dependencies, choose a test double, and pick the boundary cases for a rule.
lessons.nextAction: Draw layers and ports, and check that the dependencies point the right way.

blocks.text: Here is a function that reads the clock, saves a record to a database and sends an email. To test it, the test has to have a database, a mail server and the right date, and the function has been written so that none of them can be replaced. The usual response is to look for a better test tool, but the problem is in the design: the function chooses its own dependencies.

That function can be made testable by changing what it is given. The result is faster tests, and also a design that a reviewer can check cheaply, which matters more when some of the code was written by a tool.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to place a seam, pick a stub, a fake or a mock for a test, and choose the boundary cases that pin down a rule.

recap.keyIdea: Code is testable when it is given its dependencies, and the best tests are many fast ones of a pure core.

blocks.text: Passing a dependency in as an argument creates a seam at which a test can substitute a stub, a fake or a mock, and a pure core of decisions needs none of them. Tests should sit mostly at the base of the pyramid and, for a rule such as age >= 18, at its boundary, where the cases 17 and 18 show the answer change.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson arranges the code into layers and ports, and checks which way each dependency points.

lessons.title: Layers and ports

lead.text: A system is built as four layers: presentation, application, domain and data. The rule in this design is that each layer may use only the layer directly beneath it.

reveal.text: Relaxed layering lets a layer reach past the one below it, and a later question counts those arrows.

steps.headline: In a layered design each layer depends on the layer below, and strictness limits how far a change can spread.

lead.text: A **layered** design groups code into layers, such as presentation, application, domain and data, with each allowed to depend on the layer below. The arrows run one way, from the top down, which makes the order of the code easy to follow. In a strict design a layer calls only the one directly beneath it, giving three arrows for four layers, and in a relaxed design a layer may also skip a layer, which allows six.

The count is the one from the lesson on coupling, applied to layers: n × (n − 1) ÷ 2 arrows when everything may reach everything below. Each arrow is a place where a change can spread, so strict layering has fewer of them, and relaxed layering gives callers a shortcut at the price of more dependencies.

diagram.alt: Four layers stacked: presentation, application, domain and data. In a strict design each layer depends only on the layer directly below. In a relaxed design a layer may also depend on layers further down.
diagram.caption: Allowed dependencies in a strict and in a relaxed layering. Use the buttons to compare.

reveal.text: The strict count is only one less than the number of layers.

steps.headline: Layers do not guarantee low coupling, since the data layer at the bottom sets the shape that every layer above must use.

lead.text: Layers promise that the top does not know the bottom, but a layered design with the database at the foot makes everything depend on it indirectly. A column called cust_nm becomes order.cust_nm in the domain, then dto.cust_nm in the application, and then a field in the JSON that clients read. The first view of the figure shows the result: rename the column and every layer has to change, because each has copied a name that belongs to storage.

The repair is the one from dependency inversion. The domain defines the interface it needs, such as a Repository for orders, and this interface is a **port**. The database code becomes an **adapter** that implements the port, and it alone knows the column names, as the second view shows. The domain speaks in its own words, as the lesson on domain modelling advised, and the adapter translates.

afterFigure.text: The arrow between the domain and the data now points toward the domain, since the adapter imports the port that the domain owns.

diagram.alt: A field called cust_nm in a database column, and how far it spreads. With plain layers the name appears in the domain, the application and the JSON, so renaming the column changes every layer. With a port, only the data adapter knows the column name and the layers above use customer_name.

steps.headline: The hexagonal architecture puts the domain in the middle, with adapters that drive it on one side and adapters it drives on the other.

lead.text: Alistair Cockburn described the **hexagonal architecture** in 2005, and its picture is the domain in the middle with ports around its edge. On the left are the adapters that *drive* the application: a web interface, a command-line tool, a test. On the right are the adapters that the application *drives*: a database, a mail server. Every adapter plugs into a port, so each can be replaced without a change to the domain, and the number of sides of the hexagon is only a way of drawing room for ports.

Both views of the figure use the same domain. In production, HTTP and the command line call the same use cases, and the application stores orders in a database and sends mail. In a test, the driver is the test itself and the database is an in-memory fake. This is why such a design is easy to test, and why one set of business rules can serve several inputs.

afterFigure.text: The ring versions that followed, Jeffrey Palermo's onion architecture of 2008 and Robert Martin's clean architecture of 2012, share one rule: source-code dependencies point inward, toward the domain, and never outward to frameworks. This is the **dependency rule**.

diagram.alt: A hexagon with the domain and its use cases in the middle. On the left, adapters such as HTTP and a command line drive the application. On the right, adapters such as a database and mail are driven by it. A second view replaces the driving side with tests and the database with an in-memory fake.
diagram.caption: Adapters on both sides of the same domain. Use the buttons to switch what is plugged in.
